alternative: Immutable value objects plus explicit copies at the write boundary: frozen dataclasses/namedtuples/tuples/bytes with dataclasses.replace or copy.replace (3.13) for updates; for bulk buffers let a library own the sharing (pandas copy-on-write mode, NumPy views over a base buffer, PyArrow buffers).
idiom_name: none - immutable value objects and explicit replace()/copy (no reliable sharing test)
implementation_notes: Transparent copy-on-write is not implementable in Python: no hook fires before a mutation, mutable containers alias by reference, and the only sharing signal is CPython's sys.getrefcount, which is implementation-specific and inflated by temporary references. The stdlib copy primitives are eager - copy.copy/copy.deepcopy duplicate at call time, and the docs warn that deepcopy may copy too much, such as data intended to be shared between copies - while copy.replace (3.13) is the language-appropriate non-destructive write. Model values as immutable objects and rebind at the write edge; keep a hand-written handle/body only inside a boundary type you fully control (an explicit shared flag plus detach() in every mutator), and leave large-buffer sharing to a data library whose copy decisions are part of its documented semantics.
pitfalls: A frozen dataclass is only shallowly immutable: a list or dict field can still be mutated through the frozen instance unless it is copied in __post_init__.
sys.getrefcount() cannot serve as an 'am I shared?' test - it is CPython-specific and includes the temporary reference created by the call itself.
copy.deepcopy is not a write path: it duplicates eagerly (including data meant to be shared), so calling it on every mutation is just copying with extra steps.
memoryview and NumPy views share the buffer: a write through one view is visible to every holder, so a view is not a private copy.
